separator combined with is_flag, count, or nargs != 1 raises TypeError at construction. An empty-string separator raises ValueError.
interaction_rules: Source precedence is unchanged (command line > env > default_map > default > prompt). Splitting applies to whichever source wins, so get_parameter_source still reports a single source.
multiple=True together with a separator is allowed and behaves the same, because a separator already implies repeatable occurrences.
Shell completion completes the segment after the last separator and keeps the earlier segments as a prefix. `--tag x,<TAB>` with Choice(['x', 'y']) offers 'x,x' and 'x,y'.
traps: Splitting in consume_value only covers command-line and env values. A prompted answer reaches type_cast_value through prompt_for_value's value_proc (core.py:3551) as a bare string, and iterating it yields single characters. The split has to happen where every source converges, in type casting.
Leaving Option.value_from_envvar on its whitespace split_envvar_value path (core.py:3617-3619) makes TAG='a,b' a single item 'a,b', or splits 'a b' wrongly.

Passing the whole incomplete 'x,y' to Choice.shell_complete finds no prefix match, so completion goes silent after the first comma. Only the last segment should be matched, with the prefix re-attached.
Treating separator as plain multiple without splitting default_map strings sends a str through check_iter, which iterates its characters, so default_map={'tag': 'a,b'} becomes ('a', ',', 'b').
candidates.novelty_rationale: No separator parameter exists in core.py or parser.py. click-extra's MultiChoice is a type limited to choices and does not unify env, default_map, prompt and completion behaviour for arbitrary types. The space-separated variant the maintainer objected to (it needs parser changes) is deliberately out of scope.

candidates.title: mutually_exclusive= on Command: reject conflicting explicit parameters
candidates.problem: Click has no way to declare that `--json` and `--yaml` cannot be used together. Users write helpers that count set flags and raise UsageError (the gist warns its helper breaks when names are reused across contexts), or they adopt cloup's constraint system, which requires cloup.Command.
candidates.user_story: As a CLI author, I want to declare groups of parameters that cannot be given together and get a standard usage error, without hand-written counting helpers (gist exclusive() helper; cloup constraints).
behavior: Each inner sequence names parameters by their Python name (Parameter.name). After all parameters are processed in Command.parse_args, if two or more members of a group were explicitly provided, parsing fails with a UsageError (exit code 2, usage line shown).

'Explicitly provided' means ctx.get_parameter_source(name) is COMMANDLINE, ENVIRONMENT or PROMPT, i.e. `source < ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP`, the convention in ParameterSource's docstring (core.py:186-188). Values from default_map or defaults never conflict.

The message is "{hint_a} cannot be used together with {hint_b}.". The hints come from Parameter.get_error_hint(ctx), for example "'--json' cannot be used together with '-y' / '--yaml'.". The two names are the first two explicit members in the group's declared order.
Groups are checked in declaration order, and only the first violation is reported.
A name that is not a parameter of the command raises TypeError naming it when the command parses.
A boolean flag given explicitly as its false spelling (`--no-json`) still counts as provided.
interaction_rules: Eager parameters that exit (--help, --version) run before the check, so `cli --json --yaml --help` shows help.
Under ctx.resilient_parsing (shell completion) no conflict error is raised.
A missing required parameter or a conversion error raised while parameters are processed is reported before any conflict, because the check runs after the processing loop.
traps: Checking truthiness of ctx.params values instead of sources misses explicit falsy values (`--no-json`, `--count 0`). It also flags params whose default is truthy even though the user never passed them.

Treating DEFAULT_MAP as explicit makes a config-provided `json: true` conflict with a command-line `--yaml`. Click's own explicitness boundary (deprecation warning at core.py:2794-2798) excludes default_map.

Several options can share one name (feature-switch groups arbitrated in handle_parse_result, core.py:2820-2847). Iterating Parameter objects instead of names makes two spellings of one destination conflict with each other. The group members are names, resolved through ctx.get_parameter_source.

Running the check before the UNSET-to-None loop and the arbitration finishes can read a provisional source from a parameter that lost arbitration. It must run after every parameter's handle_parse_result has completed.
candidates.novelty_rationale: Grepping for 'mutually' or 'constraint' in src/click finds nothing. Cloup's constraints need cloup.Command and click-option-group needs its own group decorators. This is a single declarative Command argument based on click's existing ParameterSource explicitness rule.

candidates.title: click.config_option(): load a JSON config file into default_map
candidates.problem: Click only offers the low-level Context.default_map. Every app that wants `--config FILE` writes an eager callback that reads the file and fills ctx.default_map, often mutating the shared context_settings dict, breaking subcommand sections, or failing on a missing default path (jwodder gist and blog post).
candidates.user_story: As a CLI author, I want `@click.config_option(default=<app-dir path>)` so users can set any option's default in a JSON file, with subcommand sections, without me reimplementing the default_map plumbing.
public_interface: click.config_option(*param_decls: str, **kwargs) -> Callable[[FC], FC]   # default decl '--config'; defaults: is_eager=True, expose_value=False, type=click.Path(dir_okay=False), help='Read option defaults from a JSON file.'
behavior: The file must contain a JSON object. Its keys are parameter names, and nested objects are sections for subcommands keyed by subcommand name, the same shape as default_map.
Loaded values become ctx.default_map entries. They are used when a parameter is not given on the command line or by env var, and get_parameter_source reports DEFAULT_MAP.
An existing ctx.default_map (from context_settings or inherited from a parent group) is merged with the file. Nested mappings are merged recursively, and file values win on conflicts.

A path given on the command line or by env var that does not exist fails with BadParameter "Invalid value for '--config': File 'x.json' does not exist.". A missing file at the option's default path is silently ignored.
Invalid JSON or a non-object top level fails with BadParameter "Invalid value for '--config': Could not load config file 'x.json': <reason>".
Applied on a group, the file configures that group's parameters and, through sections, its subcommands. `{"verbose": true, "sync": {"jobs": 4}}` gives the group --verbose=True and `cli sync` jobs=4.
interaction_rules: Precedence is unchanged: command line > env var > config file (default_map) > parameter default > prompt-on-missing.

Because the option is eager, it is processed before all non-eager parameters, so they see the merged default_map. Subcommand contexts derive their section from parent.default_map.get(info_name) when they are created (core.py:393-397), which happens after the group's parse.
String values for multi-value parameters are split the way default_map strings already are (core.py:2553-2556). Lists are used as-is.
traps: Updating ctx.default_map in place mutates the dict passed via context_settings, because make_context copies context_settings shallowly into Context kwargs (core.py:1330-1365). The values then leak into the next invocation of the same command object. A new merged dict must be assigned.

Using click.Path(exists=True) as the type makes a missing *default* config path a hard error on every run. Existence has to be checked in the callback, using ctx.get_parameter_source to tell DEFAULT from COMMANDLINE/ENVIRONMENT.
Replacing ctx.default_map instead of merging drops the section a subcommand inherited from its parent's default_map, as well as app-provided defaults.

Leaving is_eager False means parameters declared before --config, or given earlier on the command line, are processed before the map is loaded (iter_params_for_processing, core.py:147-171) and silently ignore the file.
candidates.novelty_rationale: src/click has no config loader, only get_app_dir and default_map. click-extra's config_option is a large multi-format system with auto-discovery. This is a minimal stdlib-only core decorator that fixes the default_map sharing and missing-default pitfalls the gist runs into.

candidates.title: Choice(enum_by_value=True): match Enum members by their values
candidates.problem: Choice.normalize_choice always uses Enum.name (types.py:416), so `Choice(Format)` makes users type 'TEXT' rather than the value 'text'. Help defaults also show the member name (core.py:3471-3472), and prompts list repr-like 'Format.TEXT' strings (termui.py:117-118).
candidates.user_story: As a CLI author passing an Enum to click.Choice, I want users to type the member values ('json', 'yaml') everywhere: parsing, help, prompts, errors and completion (click-extra EnumChoice).
public_interface: click.Choice(choices, case_sensitive: bool = True, *, enum_by_value: bool = False)
behavior: With enum_by_value=True, Enum members normalize to str(member.value) instead of member.name. Non-Enum choices are unaffected. `--fmt json` with class Fmt(Enum): JSON='json' returns Fmt.JSON.
The metavar, invalid-choice message, missing message and shell completion all use the values: "'xml' is not one of 'json', 'yaml'.", metavar '[json|yaml]', completion of 'j' gives 'json'.
case_sensitive=False casefolds the value, so 'JSON' is accepted.
Int-valued enums match on the string form: '1' selects Level.LOW with value 1.
The help default for an option whose default is an enum member shows the value when the option's type is a by-value Choice: '[default: json]'.
The prompt's choice list shows the normalized values: 'Format (json, yaml): '. An empty answer with an enum default returns that member.
interaction_rules: Every value source goes through Choice.convert, so env var, default_map and string defaults all match on values. A default given as an enum member converts to itself.
ctx.token_normalize_func still applies after the value is taken, as in normalize_choice today.
Choice.to_info_dict is unchanged, and with enum_by_value=False behaviour is identical to today.
traps: Changing only normalize_choice leaves Option.get_help_extra printing default_value.name (core.py:3471-3472), so help says 'default: JSON' while parsing only accepts 'json'.
termui._build_prompt lists `map(str, type.choices)` (termui.py:117-118), which renders 'Fmt.JSON'. The prompt must list the normalized values for by-value choices or it advertises inputs that fail.
Comparing the raw member.value with the input string fails for non-str values (int enums). Normalization must stringify the value, as it does for non-enum choices.
Adding enum_by_value to Choice.to_info_dict breaks the exact dicts in tests/test_info_dict.py.
candidates.novelty_rationale: Choice matches Enum only by name (types.py:416). click-extra's EnumChoice is a separate type with aliases. This adds a flag on the core type and keeps help defaults and prompts consistent, which a subclass that only overrides normalize_choice cannot fix.

candidates.title: Context(help_styles=...) to colour headings and terms in --help
candidates.problem: HelpFormatter writes plain text only (formatting.py:204-271), and Context.make_formatter passes only widths (core.py:638-650). Coloured section headings and option names need click-help-colors, rich-click or a custom formatter_class.
candidates.user_story: As a CLI author, I want bold or coloured 'Usage:'/'Options:' headings and coloured option and command names in --help via a context setting (click-help-colors: 'Colorization of help messages in Click').
public_interface: click.Context(..., help_styles: cabc.Mapping[str, cabc.Mapping[str, t.Any]] | None = None)   # keys 'heading' and 'term', values are click.style kwargs; inherited from parent
click.HelpFormatter(indent_increment=2, width=None, max_width=None, *, heading_style: Mapping | None = None, term_style: Mapping | None = None)
behavior: heading_style is applied with click.style to each section heading including its colon ('Options:', 'Commands:', 'Positional arguments:', custom sections) and to the default 'Usage:' prefix.
term_style is applied to the first column of every definition list, i.e. option specs, argument metavars and command names. The description column is unstyled.
Column alignment and wrapping use visible width, so styled help with ANSI stripped is identical to the unstyled help at the same terminal width.
Styles show only when colour is enabled. --help is echoed with ctx.color, so runner.invoke(cli, ['--help'], color=True) contains ANSI codes and color=False gives byte-identical plain output.
Subcommand contexts inherit help_styles from the parent unless they set their own, in the same way as color.
An explicit prefix passed to HelpFormatter.write_usage is written as given and is not restyled.
interaction_rules: Usage lines printed inside usage errors come from ctx.get_usage(), which uses the same formatter, so the 'Usage:' prefix is styled there too and stripped by echo with ctx.color when colour is off.
Context.make_formatter passes heading_style/term_style only when help_styles is set, so custom formatter_class subclasses with the old __init__ signature keep working.
Unknown keys in help_styles are ignored, while invalid style arguments raise the same error click.style raises.
traps: Measuring row widths before styling and padding the styled strings with len() misaligns columns. Padding and the col_max comparison must use term_len on the styled term (formatting.py:248-256), and widths must be measured on what is actually written.
Always passing new keyword arguments from Context.make_formatter breaks every user formatter_class whose __init__ only accepts width/max_width.
Styling the heading before write_heading appends ':' leaves the colon unstyled, or doubles it if the style is added around 'Options:' and the colon is appended again.
Not inheriting help_styles in Context.__init__ makes subcommand --help unstyled while the group's help is styled.
candidates.novelty_rationale: HelpFormatter has no style hooks, and core.py calls style() only for deprecation messages. click-help-colors and rich-click provide their own Group/Command classes or renderers. This is a small context setting for the stock formatter that keeps alignment and colour stripping correct.

input.prompt: List related issues and outcomes

content:
**Issue #2771 in pallets/click** asks for options with `nargs=-1` to accept an arbitrary number of values, separated by a non-whitespace character such as a comma or pipe. The goal is to let users write `--option 1,2,3` or `--option 1|2|3` instead of repeating the option.

**Status: Open.** The page shows no assignee, milestone, or linked pull request.

- **Discussion:** Maintainers were skeptical. AndreasBackx said comma-separated values were already possible (`1,2,3`) and that the project should focus on other open issues first. davidism explained that Click's parser only sees tokens from the shell, so `1, 2, 3` (with spaces) would require substantial parser changes. He also suggested a callback that splits values on `|` as a workaround that works today.
- **Milestone history:** It was added to the 9.0.0 milestone in November 2024 and removed in October 2025.
- **Partial workaround:** In June 2026, a contributor released a `MultiChoice` parameter type in the separate Click Extra package, which supports comma-separated values. The contributor noted that the unquoted space-separated form (`--ids 1 2 3`) would still need core parser changes.

Yes. Cloup provides `mutually_exclusive` in `cloup.constraints`. The docs describe it as a rephrased version of `AcceptAtMost(1)`, so at most one of the grouped parameters may be set.

It isn't declared on the `Command` itself. You apply it in one of three ways:

1. **On an option group:** pass it as the `constraint` argument of `@option_group` or `OptionGroup`.
2. **With `@constraint`:** stack `@constraint(mutually_exclusive, [...])` on the command function, listing the parameters by destination name. For example:
   ```python
   @constraint(mutually_exclusive, ['arg', 'one', 'two'])
   ```
3. **As a decorator:** use `@mutually_exclusive(...)` with parameter decorators as arguments. This is syntactic sugar over `@constraint`:
   ```python
   @mutually_exclusive(
       option('--one'),
       option('--two'),
       option('--three'),
   )
   ```

To list the constraint in the command's help, set `show_constraints=True` on the command.

Click's built-in `click.Path` has no option that requires a file to be absent. Its `exists` parameter only checks for presence, and `False` means existence is simply not checked.

- The Click parameter docs describe `exists` as a flag meaning the path must exist. The standard definition for the click.Path exists parameter is that for True a location must exist, but False means it is not required to exist (not that it is required to not exist).
- A common workaround is a custom subclass. The LSST Butler project's `MWPath` overrides click.Path to implement file-does-not-exist checking. Its `exists` argument takes three values: True means the location must exist, False means the location must not exist, and None means it may exist or not.
- Other option: validate inside the command yourself, for example by calling `os.path.exists()` or `Path.exists()` and raising `click.BadParameter` if the file is already there.

I didn't find a Click release that adds a "must not exist" mode, so treat the subclass or manual check as the practical options.

Yes. Click Extra provides a `--color` option and respects both `NO_COLOR` and `FORCE_COLOR`.

**`--color` option**
- It is a tri-state option, `--color[=WHEN]`, where `WHEN` is `auto`, `always`, or `never`. A bare `--color` means `always`.
- `--no-color` is an alias of `--color=never`.
- The option is eager and sets `ctx.color`, which Click's `echo()` reads.
- The default is `auto`, which uses color on a terminal and strips it when output is piped.
- GNU-style synonyms are accepted as hidden aliases: `yes`/`force` for `always`, `no`/`none` for `never`, and `tty`/`if-tty` for `auto`.

**Environment variables**
- `NO_COLOR` turns color off, whatever its value.
- `FORCE_COLOR` turns color on. A falsy value (`0`, `false`, `no`, `off`) turns it off instead. The docs note this deliberately differs from force-color.org, which forces color for any non-empty value.
- Other recognized variables include `CLICOLOR`, `CLICOLOR_FORCE`, `LLM`, and `COLOR`.
- An empty value is treated as unset, and plural spellings like `NO_COLORS` or `FORCE_COLORS` also work.
- If variables conflict, the one turning color on wins.
- An explicit `--color` or `--no-color` on the command line overrides the environment.
- A `TERM` of `dumb` or `unknown` disables color under `auto`, even on a TTY. A variable that turns color on still overrides this.
- CLI-prefixed variables such as `MYCLI_NO_COLOR=1` apply only to a CLI named `mycli`.

**The request (septatrix, Aug 2021):** Let `@click.command()` run `async def` callbacks directly, so users don't need a wrapper that calls `asyncio.run()`. **Maintainer responses:**

He pointed out that Click's API is entirely sync, so async support would mean duplicating objects, and that mixing sync and async `ParamType` conversions creates ambiguous dispatch and overhead. He asked for a concrete use case: "What _specifically_ do people want to do that they can't do right now?" Later he said the most plausible addition would be auto-starting an event loop for `async def` callbacks, with an overridable loop-spawning method like Flask's. He also noted that `asyncio.run()` already works.
- **ThiefMaster** questioned whether argument parsing needs async at all.

**Other participants:**

The Cloup option groups API organizes `--help` output into titled sections, and the main entry point is the `@option_group` decorator.

- **Decorator signature:** `@option_group(title, *options, help=None, constraint=None, hidden=False)`. `help` can be passed as a keyword or as the second positional argument.
- **Options:** Each item can be a `cloup.option`, a `click.option`, or any similar decorator. Since v0.9, one decorator can add several options.
- **Constraint:** An optional constraint, such as `RequireAtLeast(1)`, is described in brackets next to the group title.
- **Hidden:** Setting `hidden=True` hides the group and all of its options from help.
- **Default group:** Options not assigned to a group appear in a default group, titled "Other options" or just "Options" if it is the only group.
- **Alignment:** Groups are aligned by default. Setting `align_option_groups=False` on the command, or as a Context setting (v0.8.0+), formats each group independently. Lowering `col1_max_width` (default 30) can also help.
- **Alternative APIs:**
  - `OptionGroup` lets you call `.option()` on a group object, avoiding extra indentation. This is syntactic sugar for `cloup.option(..., group=...)`.
  - `cloup.Option` with a `group=` argument works for building a `Command` directly without decorators.
- **Reuse:** Storing the result of `option_group(...)` in a variable lets you apply the same group to several commands. Each application creates new group and option objects.
- **Internals:** Each option gets a `group` attribute, and `Command` groups options by it. `OptionGroupMixin` overrides `format_options` to render the sections.
- **Requirements:** `OptionGroupMixin` is required, and `ConstraintMixin` is needed for constraints. Since v0.14.0, `cloup.Group` supports option groups and constraints too.

**click-help-colors** adds color to Click's help output. You apply it by passing a custom class to Click's `cls` parameter.

**Configuration (class arguments)**
- Use `HelpColorsGroup` for groups and `HelpColorsCommand` for individual commands.
- `help_headers_color` sets the color of section headings.
- `help_options_color` sets the color of the options list.
- `help_options_custom_colors` is a dictionary that overrides colors for specific items. On a group, the keys are subcommand names (e.g., `'command3': 'red'`). On a command, the keys are option flags (e.g., `'--count': 'red'`).
- Setting a color argument to `None` turns off that colorization for the command.
- Command-level settings override group-level ones.

**Example**
```python
@click.group(cls=HelpColorsGroup, help_headers_color='yellow', help_options_color='green')
```

**Other features**
- A `version_option` decorator colors version output. It accepts `version_color`, `prog_name_color`, and `message_color` arguments, plus `message` for custom text.

**Installation**
- `pip install click-help-colors`

The search turned up a few ways to load a config file into Click defaults, mostly through `ctx.default_map`.

- **Core mechanism:** Click's `default_map` on the context is the key feature for setting option values from a config file. Click also runs those values through the normal type conversion and validation. (The key feature of Click that will allow us to set parameter values from a configuration file is the default_map attribute of click.Context; Click will map values in default_map through the parameters' normal type conversion & validation routines.)
- **Eager callback pattern:** A custom `--config` option needs to be eager, so its callback fills `ctx.default_map` before other options read their defaults. (This is described in the same jwodder gist, item 4-3.)
- **click-config-file package:** Its `configuration_option` decorator adds a `--config` option by default and supports implicit config discovery. You can turn discovery off with `implicit=False`, or pass a custom provider such as a JSON reader. (The default name for the configuration file option is --config; Disable implicit configuration file discovery appears in the tessl registry summary of the package.) Its default file format is Configobj's unrepr mode, so JSON requires a custom provider (By default click-config-file supports files formatted according to Configobj's unrepr mode.).
- **click-extra's `config_option`:** It loads file values into `default_map`, so Click reports them as the DEFAULT_MAP source, placed below environment variables in precedence (Configuration file values are loaded into Click's default_map, so they are reported as ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP and sit below environment variables in the hierarchy.).
- **Known issue:** With `show_default=True`, values that come from `default_map` may not appear correctly in `--help` output (Click issue #2632, item 7-1).
- **Auto-loading caveat:** The typed-settings library does not load files from default paths automatically with its default loaders, so you have to configure that yourself (item 3-4).

**MultiChoice**

- **Separator:** Defaults to `,` and can be any single character. It also drives the metavar, so `[a,b,c]` becomes `[a;b;c]` with `;`. Consecutive or trailing separators are dropped, and surrounding whitespace is trimmed.
- **Case and output:** Matching is case-insensitive unless `case_sensitive=True`. The returned tuple uses the canonical values from `choices`.
- **Config and defaults:** An already-parsed tuple or list isn't split again, but it is still validated. The docstring says this covers values coming from a configuration file as well as CLI-declared defaults.
- **No choices:** If `choices` is empty, `MultiChoice` only parses and leaves validation to your code. The metavar then falls back to Click's default, such as `MULTI`.

The search turned up one main answer: the **cloup** extension for Click. It adds named help sections for subcommands. Plain Click's own help output lists subcommands under one "Commands:" heading, as its documentation example shows.

- **Section objects:** cloup's `Section` class is a set of subcommands that appear under the same help heading in a group's help. It is defined by a title, a set of commands, and an is_sorted flag.
- **Creating sections:** Cloup's `Group.section()` method creates a new section, adds it to the group, and returns it. The `add_section` method can also attach an existing section object, and the same section object can only be added once.
- **Adding commands:** The `add_command` method takes an optional `section` argument, and it adds a subcommand to the group.
- **Ordering:** The default section is the last shown section in the help, and its commands are listed in lexicographic order.
- **Alignment:** The `align_sections` option controls whether the columns of all sections line up. It sets whether the columns of all subcommands' help sections are aligned.

Cloup's documentation describes these as versions 0.5.0 and later. I did not check the current release notes, so confirm the version you're using before relying on these method names.

The search turned up a common pattern: subclass `ClickException` and override `show()` so the message is printed in red.

- **Red-message subclass:** A project's CLI defines a `ClickException` subclass whose docstring says it displays errors in red. Its `show()` method is where the coloring happens. Custom exception class for displaying errors in red color.
- **How the color is applied:** The same project's source, in another version, prints the message with `click.secho` and `fg='red'`, writing to stderr. Display the error message in red. The `secho` call sits in that `show()` override (click.secho(self.format_message(), fg='red', file=sys.stderr)).
- **Default behavior:** Click's stock `ClickException.show()` writes the message to stderr with an "Error:" prefix and no red styling. Newer Click versions also cache the color setting at construction time and pass it to `echo`, so the output respects color settings (cache the color settings here to be used later on (in `show`)).
- **Pitfall:** Passing an exception object to `click.style` fails, because click.style does not support an Exception as an argument, hence it raises an error on its own. Convert the exception to a string first, or use `click.secho` on the formatted message.

I did not find an official Click doc describing a built-in color option for `ClickException`. The red output comes from overriding `show()` yourself. This is based on one search, so check the Click docs for your version before relying on the exact code.

The search turned up no Click-specific documentation for a `--color always|never|auto` option or for how Click handles `NO_COLOR` and `FORCE_COLOR`. Here's what the results do cover:

- **Click's default behavior:** Click's API docs say Click will remove color if the output does not look like an interactive terminal by default. The `color` parameter lets code force colors on or off.
- **Click has no standard env-var handling:** A Click GitHub issue proposes semantics that treat `FORCE_COLOR`, `CLICOLOR_FORCE`, and `--color=always` as forcing color on, and `CLICOLOR=0`, `FORCE_COLOR=0`, and `--color=off` as forcing it off (FORCE_COLOR ≠ 0, CLICOLOR_FORCE ≠ 0, --color=always force it to be on). A separate Lightrun thread notes there's no real standard for this, and users write their own workarounds by setting `ctx.color` themselves.
- **The `--color` flag is an app-level pattern:** pip-tools PR #2041 added a `--color` and a `--no-color` flag because click uses auto-detection to only enable colors when writing to a TTY. The flag was added in the application, not provided by Click.

**What it does:** click-option-group is a Python package that extends Click by adding option groups, which Click lacks. You use the `optgroup` decorators to group options under labeled headings in `--help` output. It also supports group behaviors such as mutually exclusive options, as in the `RequiredMutuallyExclusiveOptionGroup` example.

**Stars:** The repository has 121 stars, 4 watchers, and 16 forks.

**Why it exists:** Click has no built-in way to group options. The README says Click "has no the functionality for creating option groups." Grouping helps structure a CLI and lets you define relationships between options, which the standard library's argparse already supports. Several Click users have requested this feature in issues on the Click project. The package aims to provide extensible group options with an API that closely resembles Click's.

Cloup's subcommand sections let you split a `Group`'s subcommands into several labeled groups in its help output. The page describes this as "the possibility of organizing the subcommands of a `Group` in multiple help sections." It also lists two ways to add sections: adding full sections at once, or adding subcommands one at a time.

The page doesn't give a detailed reason for the feature. It frames sections as part of Cloup's broader goal of making Click "more expressive and configurable," alongside option groups and constraints. The page doesn't say what limitation in Click it addresses.

**Status:** Open. Click has no built-in way to group options or arguments under headed sections in `--help`. The issue carries the `help output` label, added January 2025.

**The request (Diaoul, July 2015):** The author had many options and wanted to classify them under headings in the help output, like argparse's `add_argument_group`.

**Maintainer and contributor responses:**
- **untitaker (2015):** Said it wasn't supported yet. He thought it belonged in Click but could also be a third-party extension. He suggested subclassing `Command` and overriding `format_options`.
- **Diaoul (2015):** Proposed a decorator-based API, first `option_group`, then renamed to `section` so it could also cover arguments. untitaker agreed nesting should be forbidden at first.
- **jtrakk (2019):** Shared a subclassing workaround for grouping subcommands into sections.
- **chrisjsewell (2019):** Proposed a `help_group` option on a custom option class plus a custom `format_options`. This became the most cited approach.
- **jcrotts (maintainer, 2019):** Was not sure it belonged in core, since subclassing handles it. Suggested documenting examples instead.
- **thedrow (2019–2020):** Favored adding chrisjsewell's approach to core as a common use case.

- **espdev (2020):** Author of `click-option-group`. Endorsed the section-decorator API idea and planned to borrow ideas from cloup.
- **davidism (July 2020):** Removed the `enhancement` and `contrib-idea` labels.
- **reitzig (2022):** Noted that `rich-click` implements something similar.

**Outcome:** No core Click feature has been merged. Users rely on subclassing examples in the thread or on third-party packages: cloup, click-option-group, and rich-click.

The search turned up a clear pattern for making a Click error print in red: subclass `ClickException` and override `show()`. I didn't find an official Click doc describing a built-in color option.

- **Default behavior:** In Click's own source, the base `show()` writes the message to stderr with an "Error:" prefix (echo("Error: {}".format(self.format_message()), file=file)).
- **Red output in practice:** A Python project (hfutils) defines a `ClickErrorException` subclass for red errors. Its `show()` method calls click.secho(self.format_message(), fg='red', file=sys.stderr), which is the same override approach you'd use yourself.
- **How Click handles it:** When a `ClickException` reaches the top level, Click calls its `show()` method and then exits with the exception's `exit_code` (invoke the ClickException.show() method on it to display it and then exit the program with ClickException.exit_code). So you can customize the display, the exit status, or both.
- **Caveat from a user report:** One GitHub issue notes that raising `ClickException` inside a prompt stops the prompt and makes the user restart the command (it gives me my error, but stops the prompt, so i have to start from the beginning). This matters if you're validating input interactively.

This is a tutorial gist by John T. Wodder II, dated 2020-07-17, on loading default option values for Python command-line apps built with the Click library. It shows how to read those defaults from an INI config file.

The core mechanism is Click's `default_map` attribute on the context. As the article puts it, "Any values set in this dict before parameters are processed will become the parameters' new default values." Click also converts these values through each parameter's normal type handling, so a string like `"5"` becomes an integer for an `int` option.

The gist walks through:

- **A `--config` option** that is eager, so it runs before other options, and whose callback loads the INI file's `[options]` section into `default_map`.
- **Command-line precedence:** options passed on the command line override values from the config file.
- **Error handling:** an invalid value in the config file produces a usage error rather than a stack trace.
- **Naming rules:** config keys must match the function parameter names, with hyphens converted to underscores.
- **Command groups:** nested sections like `[options.bar.baz]` pass defaults to subcommands and sub-subcommands.

It includes sample scripts and example terminal output so readers can see how each behavior works. The author notes the approach is simple to implement by hand, which helps when existing libraries don't fit a project's needs.

The search turned up a consistent pattern for building a `--config` option in Click that feeds `default_map`.

- **Core mechanism:** Click's `Context.default_map` is what lets a config file supply option defaults. A callback can write values into it, and Click runs them through the normal type conversion and validation before passing them to the command callback.
- **Eager option:** The `--config` option has to be eager so it runs before the other options read `default_map`. A common pattern is an INI-based example where the callback loads the file and sets `ctx.default_map`, with a fallback default filename.
- **Merging instead of replacing:** The aiida-core and Typer examples initialize `ctx.default_map` if it is empty and then call `update()` with the loaded config. This keeps existing defaults rather than overwriting them.
- **Ready-made options:** Click Extra provides a `config_option` decorator. Its callback is eager by default so it can set the CLI's default_map before other parameters are processed.
- **Typer variant:** The typer-config package uses the same approach, where the config option is marked eager and the callback mutates the underlying Click context's default_map.

The sources are community posts, library source, and a Stack Overflow mirror, not Click's official docs. The main Click reference on this is its documentation on `default_map` in the context.

The page explains how Click Extra resolves color from these sources, and how that relates to Click's own color handling.

- **`NO_COLOR`** turns color off whatever its value is. The page says it "Turns color off, whatever its value." An empty value counts as unset, and plural or unspaced spellings like `NO_COLORS` or `NOCOLOR` also work.
- **`FORCE_COLOR`** turns color on. A falsy value (`0`, `false`, `no`, `off`) turns it off instead, following Node.js tools. The page notes this differs from force-color.org, which forces color for any non-empty value.
- **`--color[=WHEN]`** is a tri-state option following the GNU coreutils convention. `WHEN` is `auto`, `always`, or `never`, and a bare `--color` means `always`. It is eager, so it takes effect before options like `--version`.
- **`--no-color`** is an alias of `--color=never`. It is a separate flag because Click doesn't allow `/--no-x` secondary flags on value options.
- **Precedence:** an explicit `--color` or `--no-color` on the command line always beats the environment variables. Environment variables only apply when the value comes from the built-in default.
- **Click integration:** the resolved value is stored on `ctx.color`, the standard Click attribute that `echo()` reads. `always` keeps ANSI codes, `never` strips them, and `auto` colors only on a terminal.
- **Plain Click:** the `color_option` and `no_color_option` decorators can be added to a plain `click.command`.

The search didn't return a Stack Overflow thread on this exact question, but the results point to a few ways to make Click accept enum values instead of names.

- **Built-in `click.Choice`:** Passing an Enum uses its member names as the valid choices. The Click docs describe this behavior. If an Enum is passed, the names of the enum members will be used as valid choices.
- **Click 8.2+ `EnumChoice` with `use_value`:** The Click pull request adds an `EnumChoice` type. Setting `use_value` to `True` makes it use enum values as choices instead of enum keys. The same PR notes that all enum values must be unique. Check that your Click version includes this.
- **Typer:** Typer's enum handling uses values by default, and its docs describe an `enum_by_name=True` setting for switching to names.
- **Third-party helpers:** The `enumchoice` package on PyPI takes the opposite default and uses enum member names, not enum values. The `click-extra` package offers an EnumChoice type that lets you select which part of the Enum members to use as choice strings.

For the simplest route, check whether your installed Click is 8.2 or newer and use `click.EnumChoice(MyEnum, use_value=True)`. Otherwise, a small subclass of `click.Choice` that maps values to members is the usual workaround.

Your query returned results on three approaches to colored Click help output, though none covered a specific heading-color setting for rich-click.

- **click-help-colors** (click-contrib) adds colorized help to Click. Its group and command classes take settings for header and option colors, plus custom colors for individual options. The usage example sets a header color and an option color on a group class. The repo's README includes an example that colors specific options by name. The example passes a dictionary mapping option names such as '--count' to colors.
- **rich-click** is a different project. It is a shim around Click that renders help output using Rich. Adoption is minimal: you switch the import to `import rich_click as click`. Its built-in color themes are selectable through the RICH_CLICK_THEME environment variable.
- **Cloup** is another option. Its help styling is controlled by a theme object, and its heading setting controls the style of help section headings.

If you want the heading colors specifically, I'd check the rich-click docs for its theme or style options, since my results didn't include them. I can run a narrower search on rich-click's heading-style settings if you'd like.

Maintainer David Sanders (davidism) closed the issue on April 28, 2022, marking it as a duplicate of #1498. He questioned whether NO_COLOR is "an actual accepted standard," since many projects use their own environment variables. He also noted that Click has no `--color` option, so turning color back on would still require manual work in each project.

Instead of adding built-in support, he suggested reading the variable in the application and passing it to Click's `color` parameter. He wrote that "The color parameter shown above will tell Click to not output color codes," so setting that parameter from the environment achieves the goal.

A later comment from kdeldycke pointed to a ready-made `--color/--no-color` flag in the `click-extra` package that follows the NO_COLOR convention. The issue was then locked as resolved on May 15, 2022.

**Issue #3022 in pallets/click** asks Click to support the `FORCE_COLOR` and `NO_COLOR` environment variables. Opened by ascopes on July 30, 2025, it is still open.

- **Problem:** Click decides whether to color output by checking whether the stream is a physical TTY. CI systems like GitLab, Jenkins, and GitHub Actions write logs to files, so colored output is lost there.
- **Request:** When no explicit color preference is set, `click.echo` and `click.secho` should use these variables to pick a default. Python's interpreter and libraries like `colorlog` already honor them.
- **Discussion:** On August 3, 2025, maintainer kdeldycke said his Click Extra project provides a `--color`/`--no-color` option that supports these variables. He linked three related issues (#558, #1090, #1498).
- **Later activity:** The issue was labeled as a feature and tagged "help output." Issue #2781 was marked as a duplicate of this one. On November 7, 2026, R4yHarris linked a commit referencing this issue, with a message about honoring both variables.
- **Status:** No assignee, milestone, or linked pull request is listed. One user reacted with a thumbs-up.

Maintainer mitsuhiko closed the issue on July 19, 2015, saying "There is no likely API for this and you can already manually check on this in callbacks." Earlier, he had objected that he didn't see how such a feature would work from an API standpoint. He also doubted Click could generate useful help text for these constraints, since some options only conflict under specific values of other options, which made the design too complex. He preferred a post-validation utility over an `option_group` API, which he strongly opposed.

Click's maintainers did not add config file support to Click itself. They consistently pointed to third-party packages instead.

- **untitaker (2015):** Suggested piloting the idea in a third-party package, because "the question which config format click should endorse is subject to bikeshedding."
- **RonnyPfannschmidt (2015):** Argued that if users could declare extractors, the config file format would matter less. He said the harder problem was handling overrides from system-wide config, user home, and working directories.
- **untitaker (2016):** Repeated that the feature should land in a separate package, pointing to Click's contrib page.
- **davidism (2018, Member):** Closed the issue as completed, saying Click should not handle config formats "at this time," especially the interaction of multiple formats and files. He suggested that work be left to another library or contrib package.

61	def _mask_hidden_input(message: str, value: str) -> str:
62	    """Replace occurrences of ``value`` in ``message`` with a fixed mask.
63	
64	    Both ``repr(value)`` (the form built-in :class:`ParamType` errors use
65	    via ``{value!r}``) and the raw value are masked. The raw-value pass
66	    uses word-boundary lookarounds so a substring like ``"1"`` does not
67	    match inside ``"10"``, and ``"ent"`` does not match inside
68	    ``"Authentication"``. The empty string is skipped to avoid matching
69	    at every boundary.

71	    message = message.replace(repr(value), _HIDDEN_INPUT_MASK)
72	    if value:
73	        message = re.sub(
74	            rf"(?<!\w){re.escape(value)}(?!\w)", _HIDDEN_INPUT_MASK, message
75	        )

confirmed_traps: Bool flags with secondary opts register two _Option objects that share the same `obj` and `dest` (core.py:3336-3346). So repeats have to be tracked by `obj` identity, not by spelling and not by the _Option instance. Tracking per _Option instance misses `--shout --no-shout`.
Feature switches are separate Option objects that share a dest. Keying on `dest` (which is what `state.opts` uses, parser.py:171-173) wrongly flags them as repeats.

For 'first' with a bool flag, `--no-shout --shout` must keep the const of the first occurrence. Each _Option carries its own const (parser.py:162,173), so the second _Option's process must be skipped entirely, not merely prevented from overwriting a value of the same kind.

_Option.process(value, state) never receives the spelling (parser.py:169, called at 388 and 418), so naming the second-occurrence spelling in the error means changing the signature and both call sites, in _match_long_opt and _match_short_opt.

For 'first', the repeated option's value must still be consumed from rargs. `_get_value_from_state` runs before process (parser.py:378, 413). If the skip happens before value consumption, 'b' leaks into positional args.
verdicts.integration_depth: Option.__init__ validation and to_info_dict, Option.add_to_parser (pass the policy down), _Option/_OptionParser.add_option signature, _ParsingState (a seen-objects set), and both match paths, long and short. The resilient swallowing in parse_args (parser.py:308-313) already exists and needs no change.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: Tracking repeats per _Option instance or per dest. The first misses `--shout --no-shout`; the second flags `--upper --lower`. A second likely failure: in 'first' mode, skipping `state.order.append` inconsistently, or reporting the first spelling because the opt string isn't threaded through to process.
verdicts.hardening: Define how 'first' interacts with state.order. The skipped occurrence must still be appended to state.order, because eager processing order (`--version` repeated after `--help`) is decided from order (iter_params_for_processing). Also, `-ee` short-opt clusters must count as two occurrences, with the error naming '-e'.
verdicts.reasoning: The core is a seen-set keyed by obj plus a policy branch. The traps are real, but once the spec says 'per Option object, including secondary opts', the model only needs `id(self.obj)` in state. The spelling threading touches two call sites. Several rules exist, but they mostly reduce to one well-specified mechanism. One real trap (the shared obj across two _Options) puts this at a solid 3.

confirmed_traps: The coroutine must be driven inside `with augment_usage_errors(self), ctx:` (core.py:910-911). Running it afterwards breaks get_current_context and closes resources too early, because ctx.__exit__ closes the context when depth reaches 0 (core.py:564-568).
Detection has to look at the returned object. pass_context-style wrappers hide coroutine-function-ness.

In the nested case (a loop is already running), the sub-context created by _make_sub_context (core.py:891) gets entered and exited (and closed) by the sync `with` block before the caller awaits. The returned awaitable must re-enter ctx and augment_usage_errors around the await. The callback has to be called before you know whether it is async, because sync callbacks must behave exactly as before. So the callback is called in the sync block, and the returned coroutine is wrapped in an async function that re-enters ctx. Since the first exit already ran close() on an empty stack, resources registered during the body attach to the re-entered context. Getting this right is subtle.
Chain mode collects `sub_ctx.command.invoke(sub_ctx)` results (core.py:2083-2085). This is only correct if the loop runs in Context.invoke, which Command.invoke reaches at core.py:1414.
verdicts.integration_depth: Essentially a single function, Context.invoke, but with two distinct execution paths: no running loop (asyncio.run inside the with block) and running loop (return an awaitable that re-enters the context). Result callbacks (core.py:2023) and Group.invoke inherit the fix automatically if the change stays in Context.invoke.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: The asyncio.run path will work. In the running-loop path, the model will most likely return the raw coroutine, or an awaitable that doesn't re-enter the sub-context. The sub-command then sees the parent context, or with_resource files are closed before the body runs. Also likely: using asyncio.get_event_loop() or another wrong running-loop detection, and leaking 'never awaited' warnings.
verdicts.reasoning: The first half (asyncio.run inside the with block, checking the returned value) is easy once spelled out. The nested-loop requirement is the real difficulty: the context must be re-entered when the awaitable is awaited, augment_usage_errors must be preserved, and sync-from-loop behaviour must stay unchanged. The spec states this, but the obvious implementation is subtly wrong, and tests can check get_current_context and resource cleanup inside the nested sub-command. Two interacting execution paths with real traps make this a 4.

confirmed_traps: os.stat follows symlinks and raises for dangling links (types.py:1176-1180), so the existence test must use os.path.lexists.
The check must come before the file_okay/dir_okay checks (types.py:1189-1204).
The dash shortcut (types.py:1169-1172) already bypasses everything, as long as the new check is placed inside `if not is_dash`.

Missed by the proposer: with resolve_path=True, os.path.realpath (types.py:1174) resolves a dangling symlink to its nonexistent target, so lexists(resolved) is False and the dangling link slips through. The rule 'check on the resolved path' conflicts with the 'dangling symlinks are rejected' rule, and the spec doesn't settle which wins.
rejected_traps: Adding the key to to_info_dict is only a trap if the model chooses to add it. The spec says not to, so it's a single explicit instruction rather than an interaction.
verdicts.integration_depth: A single method (Path.convert) plus __init__ validation. Prompt re-asking already works through existing BadParameter handling, so it needs no change.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: Using the existing os.stat try/except as the existence test, which lets dangling symlinks through. Or checking lexists after realpath when resolve_path=True.
verdicts.hardening: Require that with resolve_path=True the dangling-symlink check runs on the original value (lexists(value)) before resolution, while the returned path is still the resolved one. And state that must_not_exist with dir_okay=False rejects an existing directory with the 'already exists' message, not 'is a directory'. This forces explicit ordering between resolution, the lexists check and the type checks.
verdicts.reasoning: One early-return branch inside convert. Every trap disappears once the spec says 'use lexists, put the check first, inside the not-dash branch'. The only genuine interaction is resolve_path versus dangling symlinks, which the proposer missed.

The Context needs parent inheritance mirroring show_default (core.py:504-508).
The implicit count range exclusion (core.py:3494) must stay, even when show_range=True.
rejected_traps: Changing _describe_range is an unlikely choice when the spec says to decide at the Option level.
The info_dict trap is just an explicit 'don't add a key' instruction.
verdicts.integration_depth: Option.__init__ (store the attribute), Context.__init__ (parameter plus parent inheritance), and one condition in get_help_extra. All in core.py, following an existing pattern line for line.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: Forgetting parent inheritance in Context.__init__, or writing `self.show_range or ctx.show_range`, which wrongly lets ctx=False override option=True semantics. In practice it is easy to copy the show_default pattern directly.
verdicts.hardening: Let show_range also accept a string format template (e.g. show_range='{min} to {max}') that replaces _describe_range output only in help. The error message keeps the canonical form, and a string at the option level overrides a context-level False. This mirrors show_default's str/bool dual semantics (core.py:3456-3468).

format_commands computes limit from len(cmd[0]) (core.py:1995). The displayed term with ' (ci, cm)' must be used for both the row and the width.
Alias lookup must live in resolve_command/get_command so that shell completion and CommandCollection see it.

Missed: NoSuchCommand currently receives possibilities=self.commands (core.py:2111). For CommandCollection that excludes source commands, and aliases must be added to the possibilities.

rejected_traps: The info_dict key is just an explicit omission.
verdicts.integration_depth: Command.__init__, Group.resolve_command (lookup order, canonical name, suggestions), an alias scan over list_commands/get_command so that lazy groups and CommandCollection sources are covered, and format_commands (display term plus width). Chain and completion work automatically only if the change sits in resolve_command.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: Building an alias map from self.commands only, which breaks CommandCollection sources and lazy groups. Or returning cmd.name, or the alias, as cmd_name. Or getting the normalize-then-alias precedence wrong so that an alias shadows a normalized real name. Plus forgetting to put aliases in the 'Did you mean' possibilities.
verdicts.reasoning: Several rules genuinely interact: precedence across exact, alias, normalized and normalized-alias lookups; canonical-name propagation into default_map and envvars; display width; suggestions; and CommandCollection sources. They all have to be consistent across resolve_command, get_command and format_commands. Even with a precise spec, a small model will likely miss one of them (most likely CommandCollection or the canonical key).

text: I've finished reading the code for all five candidates. Scores: separator 4, mutually-exclusive 2, config-option 3, enum-by-value 2, help-styles 2.

confirmed_traps: Prompt path: Option.prompt_for_value passes value_proc=lambda x: self.process_value(ctx, x) (core.py:3551). The prompt answer is a bare string, so splitting only in consume_value misses it. The split has to happen in type casting too.

Prompt values are processed twice. prompt() returns value_proc's result (termui.py:272-278), Option.consume_value returns it as the value (core.py:3678), and handle_parse_result calls process_value again (core.py:2811). The second pass gets a tuple of already-converted items, so type_cast_value must not re-split or reject non-str items. Proposer missed this.

Option.value_from_envvar splits on whitespace whenever multiple/nargs is set (core.py:3617-3623). If separator is implemented as multiple=True underneath, the env var still goes down that path unless it is overridden.
A default_map string with multiple=True and nargs==1 is not split (core.py:2555 checks only nargs != 1). type_cast_value's multiple branch then iterates the string's characters (core.py:2617-2618).
Choice.shell_complete does a plain startswith on the whole incomplete string (types.py:508-515). 'x,' therefore matches nothing until the code splits on the last separator and re-attaches the prefix.

Missed by proposer: splitting depends on the source. Command-line occurrences arrive as a list ['a,b','c'] where each element must be split. A list/tuple default must NOT be split. type_cast_value alone cannot tell these two apart, so splitting must happen per source (consume_value for COMMANDLINE) or carry extra state.
verdicts.integration_depth: Option.__init__/_validate (core.py:3178-3198) for the TypeError/ValueError checks and forcing multi-valued behaviour. Option.add_to_parser (append action, core.py:3325-3334). Parameter.consume_value / Option.consume_value for command-line and default_map splitting. Option.value_from_envvar. type_cast_value for strings from prompt and string defaults. make_metavar for 'TEXT[,TEXT...]'. Parameter.shell_complete for segment completion. That is 5-6 cooperating paths in core.py.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: Splitting everything inside type_cast_value. That either splits list defaults that should stay intact or leaves command-line occurrences unsplit. A second likely failure is the double prompt processing: the already-converted tuple gets re-split or re-converted badly. Completion that ignores the prefix is also likely.
verdicts.reasoning: Each rule is clear on its own, but they conflict. 'Split command-line occurrences' and 'don't split list defaults' cannot both be met at a single convergence point. On top of that, the prompt path re-processes its own output, and the env-var path has its own split logic. A small model will probably pick one place to split and break one of these sources.

confirmed_traps: Using value truthiness instead of ctx.get_parameter_source misses `--no-json` and `--count 0`.
DEFAULT_MAP must count as not explicit. The `source < ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP` convention is visible at core.py:2797 and 3661.

The check must run after the processing loop in Command.parse_args (core.py:1374-1375). Placing it right after that loop also gives the intended ordering: missing-required and conversion errors come first, and eager --help exits first.

Missed: get_parameter_source returns None for unknown names. Comparing None < DEFAULT_MAP raises a raw TypeError rather than the spec'd TypeError naming the parameter, so name validation must happen before the comparison.
rejected_traps: The feature-switch trap mostly goes away because the spec names members by Parameter.name and get_parameter_source is keyed by name. Restoring sources after lost arbitration already happens (core.py:2841-2843).
'Running before arbitration finishes' is not a realistic risk. Arbitration finishes inside each handle_parse_result, and the natural place to insert the check is after the loop.
verdicts.integration_depth: A constructor argument on Command plus the decorator pass-through, and one post-loop check in Command.parse_args (core.py:1376-1386) using get_parameter_source and get_error_hint. Group.parse_args (core.py:2006) calls up through it. All of this is a single code path.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: Putting the check before the loop, or after the extra-args failure in the wrong order. Or not skipping the check under resilient_parsing. Or reporting the hints in the order given on the command line instead of declaration order.
verdicts.hardening: Prompt suppression: if a group member was already given explicitly (COMMANDLINE/ENVIRONMENT), other members of the same group must not prompt (prompt=True/required) and count as not provided. They must also not raise MissingParameter for required=True. This makes the group state visible inside Option.consume_value's prompt branch (core.py:3672-3679) and process_value's required check (core.py:2664), and it depends on processing order (iter_params_for_processing).
verdicts.reasoning: With the sources and the check location written down, this is about 15 lines in one spot. The rules (explicit-source test, declaration order, first violation wins, skip under resilient parsing) are independent and easy to follow.

confirmed_traps: Mutating ctx.default_map in place leaks into context_settings or the parent. Context.__init__ assigns the dict as-is (core.py:391-399), and an inherited section is the same object as the parent's nested dict. Merging must copy recursively.

A missing file at the default path vs an explicit one: the code has to check ctx.get_parameter_source in the callback. The source is set before process_value/callback runs (core.py:2791), so this works.
It must be eager so it runs before other parameters (iter_params_for_processing). This is copied directly from help_option/version_option (decorators.py:551-553, 619-621).

Missed: when the option has no default and is not given, the callback receives None and must skip loading. The --config value itself can also come from a parent default_map (source DEFAULT_MAP), and the spec doesn't say whether a missing file is then ignored or an error.
rejected_traps: The error-prefix formatting is not really a trap. A BadParameter raised inside the callback gets param filled in by augment_usage_errors wrapped around process_value (core.py:2785-2811), so "Invalid value for '--config'" comes for free.
verdicts.integration_depth: A new decorator in decorators.py that follows the help_option pattern, plus an export in __init__.py. All logic lives in the callback (read file, json.load, deep-merge, assign ctx.default_map). No core.py changes are needed. default_map string splitting already exists (core.py:2553-2556).
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: A shallow merge ({**old, **new}) that replaces nested subcommand sections instead of merging them. Or deep-merging into the existing dict in place, which mutates context_settings across invocations.
verdicts.hardening: Validate unknown keys: any top-level key that is neither a parameter name of ctx.command nor (for a Group) a subcommand name/alias raises BadParameter listing the keys in sorted order. Keys that map to a subcommand must hold objects. This requires walking ctx.command.params and Group.commands, and handling sections differently from scalar values.
verdicts.reasoning: Once the spec says 'eager, don't use exists=True, deep-merge into a new dict, check the source', each trap becomes a single instruction. The remaining risk is getting deep-merge-without-mutation right, which is a well-known pattern.

confirmed_traps: Option.get_help_extra hardcodes default_value.name for enums (core.py:3471-3472).
termui._build_prompt uses map(str, type.choices) (termui.py:117-118), which gives 'Fmt.JSON'.
Values must be stringified for int enums. normalize_choice already does str() for non-enums (types.py:416).
Added: _build_prompt must apply only to by-value choices. Switching it to _normalized_mapping for all Choices would casefold the prompt list for case_sensitive=False and break existing prompt tests.
Added: multiple=True with a list-of-enum default goes through the list branch at core.py:3469-3470 (str(d)) and still shows 'Fmt.JSON'. The spec doesn't cover this case.
rejected_traps: The to_info_dict trap only applies if the solver adds the key on its own. The spec says to leave it unchanged.
Enum defaults and empty prompt answers need no work. prompt round-trips the default through value_proc (termui.py:265-272) into Choice.convert, which normalizes the member itself.
verdicts.integration_depth: A constructor flag and a one-line branch in normalize_choice (types.py:416). That alone covers convert, metavar, error and missing messages, and completion. Add one branch in get_help_extra and one in _build_prompt. Three files, each change trivial.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: Forgetting the help-default or prompt-list path. Or making the prompt list show normalized values for every Choice, which breaks existing tests.
verdicts.hardening: With enum_by_value=True, input may match either a member's value or its name. Value matches take precedence when one member's name equals another member's value (e.g. A='b', B='a'). Metavar, errors, completion and help still list values only. This adds precedence inside convert while the displayed set stays different from the accepted set.
verdicts.reasoning: normalize_choice is the single funnel for nearly all behaviour, so the core change is one line. The two extra display paths are named explicitly in the spec.

confirmed_traps: make_formatter must pass the new kwargs only when help_styles is set (core.py:648-650). Otherwise custom formatter_class subclasses break.
Heading style must include the colon that write_heading appends (formatting.py:206).
help_styles must be inherited in Context.__init__, in the same way color is.
rejected_traps: The column-misalignment trap is mostly not real. measure_table already uses term_len (formatting.py:19), write_dl pads with term_len (formatting.py:255-256), and wrap_text/TextWrapper are ANSI-aware since 8.4 (formatting.py:56-60, _textwrap.py:89-154). Styling the terms before measuring aligns correctly for free.
There is no extra colour-handling work. Help and usage errors are already echoed with ctx.color (exceptions.py:105-106), so color=False strips the ANSI codes.
verdicts.integration_depth: HelpFormatter.__init__ gets two kwargs. write_heading styles f'{heading}:'. write_dl styles the first column. write_usage styles only the default prefix. Context.__init__ adds inheritance and make_formatter passes kwargs conditionally. Those are local edits in two files.
verdicts.likely_failure_mode: Always passing heading_style/term_style from make_formatter. Or styling an explicit write_usage prefix. Or missing parent inheritance when help_styles is None.
verdicts.hardening: term_style applies only to the option names in the first column, not to the metavar or separators. In '-n, --name TEXT' only '-n' and '--name' are styled; in '--shout / --no-shout' both names are styled but the ' / ' is not. This means changing Option.get_help_record/_write_opts (or passing structured terms), while alignment still uses visible width.
verdicts.reasoning: The existing ANSI-aware width infrastructure removes the main claimed trap. What's left is a handful of independent local edits that are each specified directly.
